The Big Beautiful Bill’s Medicaid reforms are a necessary correction to decades of bureaucratic bloat and fraud. Let’s cut through the noise: Medicaid was designed as a safety net for vulnerable Americans—not a slush fund for ineligible recipients or states gaming the system. The bill’s work requirements for able-bodied adults without dependents mirror successful welfare-to-work policies that lifted millions out of poverty in the 1990s.

Fraud enforcement isn’t “cruel”—it’s fiscal sanity. The SSA Death Master File provision alone would prevent $2.1B annually in improper payments to deceased individuals, per HHS audits. Meanwhile, states like Maine and Utah have already exposed 300,000+ ineligible enrollees through routine eligibility checks, proving systemic abuse exists.

The bill doesn’t “slash” Medicaid—it surgically removes waste. CBO projections showing enrollment declines ignore that 40% of Medicaid spending already goes to administrative overhead and middlemen. Redirecting those resources to actual care for seniors, disabled Americans, and working families isn’t austerity—it’s accountability. Democrats defend a broken status quo where hospitals overbill Medicaid by $60B yearly while rural clinics close. Real compassion means ensuring every taxpayer dollar reaches those truly in need.

The Big Beautiful Bill’s Medicaid reforms are a start, but let’s be real—Washington’s addiction to bloated bureaucracy won’t be cured by work requirements alone. The Energy and Commerce Committee’s $880B target for Medicaid "savings" includes eligibility crackdowns, but the real rot is deeper: Medicare fraud, hospital price-gouging, and Big Pharma’s stranglehold on drug pricing. Trump’s $1T drug cost plan hits the right nerve—pharma giants exploit patent laws and lobbyists to keep prices sky-high while taxpayers fund their monopolies.

The BBB’s focus on redirecting funds from ineligible recipients is basic fiscal hygiene, not reform. Until D.C. guts the administrative bloat enabling $273B in waste (per the bill’s own healthcare offsets), Medicaid will remain a leaky bucket.

Permanent structural change? That requires torching the entire inefficiency machine—not just trimming the edges.

Medicaid’s real problem isn’t funding—it’s fraud and bureaucratic bloat. Washington claims “cuts” when they’re just trimming waste. The BBB debate? Classic D.C. theater.

Instead of propping up failed bureaucracies, redirect those funds to veterans’ care and medical price transparency.

Let’s audit every dollar before crying about “cuts” to programs riddled with inefficiency.
